title: Remind with the Qur'an
hookLine: remind with the Qur'an whoever fears the warning (50:45)
tomorrow: Block C close: the middle of the book

lines: UMM HISHAM KNEW QAF BY HEART.
THE LAST VERSE SAYS HOW TO USE IT.
cards: A woman named Umm Hisham lived near the Prophet's mosque in Medina.

Asked years later how she knew Surah Qaf by heart, she answered, in a report in Sahih Muslim, that she learned it from the Prophet's own mouth: he recited it from the pulpit every Friday when he gave the sermon.
Week after week, the same surah, until a neighbor who never sat down to memorize it simply knew it. The last verse of that surah tells the Prophet how to use it.

teach.b: Surah Qaf ends with verse forty-five. It says, in meaning: We know best what they say, and you are not a tyrant over them, so remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning. Two halves.
The first is a limit. The Arabic word is jabbar, one who compels, who forces. The Prophet ﷺ is told plainly: that's not your role.
You can't make anyone believe. The Qur'an says this in several places; in Surah Al-Ghashiyah: remind, for you are only a reminder; you are not a controller over them. The second half is the job.
Dhakkir: remind. The root is dh-k-r, the same as dhikr, remembrance. A reminder doesn't introduce something foreign.
It assumes the listener already knows, somewhere, and has forgotten. The tool is the Qur'an itself, not anger or argument.

And it's for whoever fears the warning: the one already listening. The verse doesn't send the Prophet to chase down the unwilling. It asks him to keep the words in front of those whose hearts are turned toward them.
He did it with this very surah, every Friday, gently, until a neighbor knew it by heart without trying. Another report in Sahih Muslim says he recited Qaf at the Eid prayers too.

teach.h: SAY IT WELL; LEAVE THE HEARTS.
teach.b: It's a quiet model for anyone who loves something and wants to share it: say it, say it well, say it again, and leave the hearts to their Owner.

how: Many imams recite Surah Qaf in Friday sermons or Eid prayers following the Prophet's practice, and Muslims often share a single verse with friends and family as a gentle reminder rather than an argument.

o: warn enemies before a battle begins
force people to accept the right path
remind people of what they already know

s: 50:45 tells the Prophet to make people believe
it says he is not a jabbar, one who compels; his task is to remind.
the Prophet recited Surah Qaf in Friday sermons
Umm Hisham learned it that way, in Sahih Muslim.
dhakkir and dhikr share a root

games.q: you love a verse and want to share it. by 50:45, who is the reminder for, and how?
o: whoever fears the warning, with the Qur'an itself.
games.why: the verse limits force and sets the task: remind with the Qur'an those already listening.

practice: Bring to mind one verse or line from this path that stayed with you, Qaf, taqwa, islah, whatever it was, and say it to yourself slowly until you could say it without looking.
Then think of one person who might like to hear it, not because they need correcting, but because it's beautiful. If you pray, you can ask that it land gently.

wordCard.voice: Dhakkir: remind, the last instruction of Surah Qaf, not to force anyone, but to remind those who are listening. Today's word.
